newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian economic reform drifts while Yeltsin ill.
newsitem.headline: Russian economic reform drifts while Yeltsin ill.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's illness means many key economic decisions will not be taken, dimming prospects for Russia's recovery, economists said on Monday.
The government remains committed to reforms but without a strong leader in charge, economic policy can drift dangerously, they said.

Yeltsin, hit by heart trouble during his election campaign last June and sent to hospital with pneumonia last week, has left a government of unelected officials to run the country and make economic policy.

The Russian economy shrank by about five percent in 1996 and despite official promises that it will grow this year, only Yeltsin, who has enormous powers under the constitution, can approve many structural reforms needed to sustain recovery, analysts say.
"Until a healthy Yeltsin comes back, there are going to be questions of whether economic reform will be galvanised and driven forward," said a senior Western economist.
"(If he continued to be sick) there would be a risk we would see more of a muddling through rather than a getting to grips with structural reforms now needed in the Russian economy."
Russia has eliminated hyperinflation and won international respect from borrowers with a debut Eurobond last November but important reforms remain to be made.
Government factions are discussing and holding up reforms to the tax system, the banking system and private industry without Yeltsin to give a lead, many economists say.

Officials are debating to what extent the government should play a role in restructuring industries which have resisted reform, as companies such as carmaker AvtoVAZ, Russia's fifth biggest employer, face bankruptcy.

They predict that growth will be flat this year while much of Russian industry is caught in a barter economy, without access to credit and with enormous debts to workers, energy providers, the government and each other.
Yeltsin's administration is generally pro-reform but without Yeltsin, there is no one to choose which reforms, said Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital bank.
"There is considerable conflict between various parts of the administration but that is part of what Yeltsin was looking for -- so no one group would assume too much power," Nash said.

"There is a strong group that wants to kickstart the economy by injecting funds that would yield two to three percent growth this year but would lose the gains of the last two years (in bringing down inflation)."

Russia has not signed a diamond export deal worth billions of dollars with South Africa's De Beers because of intra-government battles and a senior central banker earlier in the month said economic policy-making was "spontaneous".

A lack of government followup meant that Yeltsin's appearance at a committee set up to deal with tax collection, which was as low as 60 percent of target levels at times last year, became a missed opportunity to assign responsibility and improve tax collection, analysts said.

U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said last week Russia needed to recapture the momentum of market reforms -- otherwise the economy would stagnate and, in particular, it neeeded to restructure the tax system.
But some analysts and foreign investors who drove Russian shares to record levels last week argue that Yeltsin's absence is irrelevant.
Miljenko Horvat, Citibank N.A. vice president and manager of a fund set up to invest in Russia, said reforms were safe.

In late June Yeltsin sacked top conservative aides, while presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, both seen as reformers, are widely regarded as the chief leaders of economic policy.
Horvat said the government and economic machine appeared to be performing adequately in Yeltsin's absence.
"It all seems fairly comfortable at the moment. Things are as good as anyone could expect."
